capabilities.target: identity provider MFA methods and temporary pass issuance

inputs.source: support tickets, including tickets emailed in by contractors

instructions.note: The prompt directs the agent to reset MFA and send the temporary pass to the ticket opener, which can treat requester-supplied identity claims as sufficient authority.
The design relies on instruction and analyst judgment to prevent misdelivery of temporary passes, with no structural binding of requester to account owner.

controls.name: Service desk analyst approval in the queue tool
controls.decay_rationale: The gate is enforced outside the model and the analyst sees the raw action target, requester, and full ticket text. Its effectiveness is reduced by very high approval volume and routine framing, but that is captured in approval_volume rather than model capability dependence.

controls.name: Bind temporary pass delivery to verified account owner destination
controls.decay_rationale: A recipient confirmation or system-of-record destination binding would prevent delivery to a requester-chosen recipient regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Analyst approval for temporary pass send action
controls.decay_rationale: A separate raw-action approval on the outbound temporary pass delivery would gate the irreversible egress sink outside the model.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket can drive directory read and irreversible delivery of a temporary pass to the requester

attack_path.note: Contractors and vendors can email tickets in, so requester-controlled content enters as untrusted.
The agent looks up directory profile and memberships for the named user.
The agent can remove MFA methods and issue a temporary pass after analyst approval.
The temporary pass is posted to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: The only declared gate covers cap.mfa_reset, not the irreversible egress sink cap.send_temp_pass. Because the design explicitly sends the temporary pass to the ticket opener rather than the account owner, the highest-risk path remains effectively ungated at the sink even though MFA reset itself is approved.

forecast.watch_signal: Any removal or narrowing of analyst review on cap.mfa_reset, or increases in unattended steps or task runtime, should trigger reassessment; model changes do not reduce this already-critical path.

evidence.observation: The prompt says to look up the user, reset MFA, and send the temporary access pass to the person who opened the ticket.
Contractors and vendors can email tickets in, making the requester field attacker-authorable.
The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner.
The analyst queue shows the reset action, target account, requester, and full ticket body, but no separate approval is described for sending the temporary pass.

recommendations.action: Bind temporary pass delivery to a verified destination from the identity system of record, not the ticket opener field.
Require a separate raw-action analyst approval for cap.send_temp_pass or remove that capability from the agent.

findings.title: Summary-gated identity action weakness: high-volume analyst approval on MFA reset is vulnerable to approval fatigue

attack_path.note: Requester-controlled ticket content can claim urgency or impersonate legitimacy.
Resetting MFA removes factors and issues a temporary pass using a shared service capability.

forecast.watch_signal: Any increase in approval volume, step limit, or removal of per-reset analyst review should trigger reassessment; the queue already processes about 400 requests per shift across two analysts.

evidence.observation: Every reset needs analyst approval before it runs.
The analyst sees the exact target account, requester, and full ticket text, so the gate is raw-action review.
Two analysts approve about 400 requests per shift and most are routine, which is high approval volume.
Requester identity can come from email sender fields for contractors and vendors, increasing risk of mistaken resets approved under routine workload.

recommendations.action: Reduce approval fatigue by requiring stronger identity verification signals in the queue and limiting analyst review load for MFA resets.

stride_coverage.rationale: No inbound peer process authentication surface for the agent itself is described in the provided artifacts.
The artifacts do not describe self-modification, mutable tool definitions, or config write paths for this agent.
No spend, loop, recursion, or service exhaustion behavior is described for this ticket resolution design.
The primary risk on this inbound boundary is malicious content injection, not disclosure from the flow itself.
The design provided does not describe ticket volume abuse causing service exhaustion or resource depletion.
The external requester is outside the assessed trust domain and no attributable logging property is evaluated for that actor.
The assessed issue is recipient misbinding, not in-transit modification of the outbound temporary pass flow.
No artifact indicates this outbound flow can be abused for service exhaustion in the current design.
No evidence shows the queue contents or approval records can be modified outside normal analyst operation.
The queue contains sensitive information, but no exposure path from the queue store itself is described in the artifacts.
The design notes high approval volume but do not show queue unavailability or capacity exhaustion as a separate risk.

rating.rationale: Manual validation applied. The design has a present critical path from untrusted ticket input to confidential identity data handling and irreversible temporary-pass delivery to the ticket opener. The declared analyst approval is a real raw-action gate on MFA reset, but its high volume weakens residual for that finding to high and it does not gate the outbound send sink. Forecast remains critical because the highest-risk path is already critical and any reduction in analyst review only worsens the identity abuse path. This assessment reflects declared design and configuration artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No tool manifest, source code, or runtime enforcement artifacts were provided, so capability wiring and absence of additional controls were assessed from prompt, queue view, and runtime notes only.
No explicit audit logging, recipient verification, or identity proofing mechanism was described; the assessment therefore treats those controls as absent rather than tested.
